clinicalPearls: Characterised by a Becker naevus, a unilateral hyperpigmented patch with hypertrichosis, usually over the shoulder or upper trunk, together with underlying developmental defects
The naevus is androgen-responsive, so it often darkens, thickens and becomes hairier around puberty and is commoner in males
Associated ipsilateral hypoplasia is typical, most often of the breast and pectoral muscle, and sometimes of the limb or shoulder girdle
Skeletal anomalies such as scoliosis, vertebral defects and limb asymmetry may accompany the cutaneous lesion
It is regarded as a mosaic disorder, with post-zygotic ACTB variants reported, explaining the segmental distribution
Underlying smooth-muscle hamartoma commonly gives the naevus a subtle perifollicular papular texture and a pseudo-Darier sign on rubbing
Management is generic: reassurance, cosmetic camouflage or laser for pigment and hair, and orthopaedic input for skeletal or breast asymmetry
reference.pathophysiology: Becker naevus syndrome is considered a mosaic condition arising from a post-zygotic variant, with somatic ACTB variants implicated in some cases, affecting a clone of cells during development. This produces a localised increase in melanisation, terminal hair growth and, frequently, a smooth-muscle hamartoma within the affected skin. The lesion's androgen sensitivity explains its accentuation at puberty and its male predominance. When the responsible clone also involves adjacent mesodermal structures, ipsilateral hypoplasia of the breast, pectoral muscle or limb and associated skeletal anomalies develop, accounting for the syndromic phenotype beyond the pigmented patch itself.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated Becker naevus without associated anomalies
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination and dermoscopy of the pigmented patch
Skin biopsy if diagnosis is uncertain or malignancy is suspected
Comparative examination for ipsilateral breast or pectoral hypoplasia
Spinal and limb radiographs where scoliosis or asymmetry is present
Ultrasound or imaging of the breast and chest wall to define hypoplasia
Orthopaedic assessment where skeletal anomalies are identified
redFlags: Progressive scoliosis or limb-length discrepancy requiring orthopaedic intervention
Significant breast or chest-wall asymmetry causing functional or psychological impact
Atypical change within the pigmented lesion raising concern for melanoma
New neurological symptoms warranting further evaluation
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good; the cutaneous lesion is benign with negligible malignant potential, and the main issues relate to cosmetic appearance and to any associated skeletal or breast asymmetry, which may need orthopaedic or reconstructive management.
pitfalls: Assuming any hyperpigmented patch with hair is benign without checking for underlying hypoplasia or skeletal defects
Confusing a Becker naevus with a congenital melanocytic naevus and overestimating melanoma risk
Overlooking scoliosis in a child with a large truncal Becker naevus
Neglecting the psychological impact of visible pigmentation and breast asymmetry
references: Happle R. Mosaicism in Human Skin
management: Manage the cutaneous naevus as cosmetically indicated, with laser hair removal for hypertrichosis and pigment-directed laser for the hyperpigmentation
Assess associated ipsilateral breast and pectoral hypoplasia, considering reconstructive or plastic surgery once breast development is complete
Monitor and treat skeletal anomalies such as scoliosis and limb asymmetry with orthopaedic input, including bracing or surgery where needed
Provide physiotherapy for musculoskeletal asymmetry and functional limitation
Reassure that the naevus itself is benign with negligible malignant potential
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across dermatology, orthopaedics and plastic or reconstructive surgery
